az_free_university_wall_e_face.blurb: A small cluster of seven routes on Mount Lemmon in the Santa Catalina Mountains, tucked on the east side of the Gumby Wall formation at roughly 7,700 feet. The climbing is a mix of bolted lines and gear routes, with four sport climbs and three trad climbs, all easy to moderate: grades run only from 5.6 to the 5.7 range. That makes it a gentle option for newer leaders or for anyone building mileage on a mountain day away from the Tucson heat. One of the lines is a multi-pitch outing, while the rest are single pitches. Reach the base by the same short walk used for the main Gumby Wall.

az_lost_wall_2.blurb: The northernmost crag in Upper Devils Canyon, on the Queen Creek side near Oak Flat. It sits apart from the canyon's other climbing, so it can be quieter than its neighbors. Seven routes, mostly bolted with lowering anchors and two traditional lines, run from about 5.6 up to the low 5.11 range, with a handful in the 5.9 to 5.10 middle. The stone is pocketed and flaky, and the face gets morning light before shade takes over later in the day. Some rock on the tops is loose and large, so helmets are wise. The trail ends in a short, unexposed scramble to the foot of the wall.

az_coop_the.blurb: A roughly 90-foot tower within Lower Devil's East, a collection of traditional-style towers across Lower Devil's Canyon in Queen Creek Canyon. Six of its seven routes are gear climbs and one is bolted. They range from 5.9 up to the 5.12 range, with most clustered around 5.9 and 5.10. The routes are on the east face and are often shaded. Rock quality here is considered among the best in the whole Lower Devil's East group. Expect a full rack, as the area favors placing your own protection and keeps bolts to a minimum. Most climbs finish on top of the tower.

az_1_people_s_court.blurb: One of the short walls at the start of the North Side in Volunteer Canyon, part of Sycamore Canyon near Flagstaff, at about 6,600 feet. It is the wall nearest the road on that side of the canyon. All seven routes are traditional lines on golden columnar basalt with very little lichen, graded from 5.10 to the 5.11 range. They run a bit shorter than most routes in the canyon. The North Side catches plenty of sun, so summer is hot and spring and fall are the best seasons. Across the canyon is a quick view of the opposite walls, which helps with picking out lines.

az_1_addendum_wall.blurb: The leftmost sector of the Dry Canyon cliff band in southern Arizona. Seven short, bolted routes on sharp gray limestone that is a touch less than vertical. Grades start at 5.9 and are concentrated in the 5.10 range, topping out near 5.11. Lines are brief, some only around 40 feet, so this is not a destination wall; it works well as a warm-up or as a last stop while hiking back down. There is probably no clear trail to the base: head up the canyon trail past its single big switchback and look for a faint path or a sharp corner on the right.

az_king_dome.blurb: The biggest and best-known outcrop in the Crown King area of the Bradshaw Mountains, at about 6,200 feet north of Phoenix. Reaching it takes a long gravel drive past the town of Crown King. The walls mostly face south, and the elevation keeps it cooler than the Valley. Seven routes, mostly bolted, with one gear crack, run from about 5.7 up to 5.10, concentrated around 5.9. Bolt spacing on the sport lines is reasonable. You can find both single-pitch and multi-pitch climbing, and a rough road gets close to the top of the crag for anyone who prefers to skip the steep hike in.
